nameStory: The Ohio buckeye earned its name from its large, glossy brown seeds that supposedly resemble the eye of a buck deer - complete with a lighter colored scar where the seed was attached to the pod. Ohio adopted this tree as its state tree, giving it the 'Ohio' part of its name, though it's also called 'fetid buckeye' because its bark and leaves smell quite unpleasant when crushed.
description: Ohio buckeye is a medium-sized deciduous tree that grows 20-40 feet tall with a rounded crown. It has distinctive hand-shaped leaves with five leaflets radiating from a central point, like fingers on an outstretched hand. In spring, it produces upright clusters of small yellowish-green flowers, followed by spiny brown capsules that split open to reveal large, shiny brown seeds. This tree is actually quite rare in New England, being far from its natural Midwest range.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive palmate leaves with exactly 5 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, each leaflet 3-6 inches long with serrated edges and a smooth texture that turns yellow-orange in fall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Upright, cone-shaped clusters of small yellowish-green flowers in late spring, each flower about half an inch across with protruding stamens that give the cluster a fuzzy appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, spiny capsules about 1-2 inches across that split into three sections, revealing 1-2 large, glossy mahogany-brown seeds with a prominent lighter-colored scar

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark that becomes scaly and furrowed with age, and when scratched or crushed, releases a distinctly unpleasant, skunk-like odor

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Large, sticky, reddish-brown winter buds that are opposite each other on the twigs and have a waxy coating that you can feel with your fingers

habitat: In New England, Ohio buckeye would most likely be found as a planted ornamental tree in parks, yards, or arboretums, since it's well outside its natural range. If naturalized, it might appear along stream banks or forest edges in areas with rich, moist soil, particularly where the soil has some limestone influence.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early with distinctive 5-leaflet pattern, followed by showy upright flower clusters in late April to May that attract bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Full leafy canopy provides dense shade, and spiny green fruit capsules develop and enlarge throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow to orange before dropping, and the spiny capsules split open to reveal glossy brown buckeye seeds that fall to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the opposite branching pattern and large, sticky reddish-brown buds that are easy to spot against winter skies.

funFact: Ohio buckeye seeds are mildly toxic and were traditionally carried as good luck charms - the name 'buckeye' became slang for people from Ohio, and the seeds were so associated with good fortune that they're still carried by some people today as pocket pieces for luck!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with horse-chestnut, which also has palmate leaves, but horse-chestnut has 7 leaflets instead of 5, larger white flower spikes, and much spinier seed capsules. Remember: 'Five for Ohio, seven for horse-chestnut.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Ohio buckeye is not closely related to the chestnut trees, but rather belongs to the soapberry family. The seeds contain saponins (soap-like compounds) that make them mildly poisonous to humans and livestock, though some Native American groups learned to process them into an edible food.
compareHints: Among buckeyes, Ohio buckeye is distinguished by having exactly 5 leaflets (not 7 like horse-chestnut) and yellowish-green flowers rather than the showy white or red flowers of other buckeye species. Its seeds are also typically smaller and less spiny than those of horse-chestnut, and it has that characteristic unpleasant odor when bruised that other buckeyes lack.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horse-chestnut is the only member of the Aesculus genus commonly found as a large tree in New England, making it fairly easy to distinguish from its relatives.
Unlike its tree-form relatives like horse-chestnut and Ohio buckeye, bottlebrush buckeye stays shrub-sized and spreads by suckers rather than growing as a single trunk.
Red buckeye is easily distinguished from other buckeyes by its bright red flowers - horse-chestnut has white flowers, Ohio buckeye has yellowish-green flowers, and yellow buckeye has yellow flowers.
